Scope: Issue content changes, status changes, and Runtime or Delivery dynamics advance one content revision, while per-user read cursors project unread state onto the board. Edge Code ownership Meaningful change → content revision Backend loop_item_unread and LoopItem mutation services User read → read revision Backend deliveries API and loop_item_unread Revision → current-user unread projection Backend LoopItemService.response_values and delivery schema Issue changed → board refresh Backend loop_item_events and Wework projectChatSocket Unread projection → card marker / read Wework CloudTodoWorkspace, CloudTodoBoardCard, and deliveries API Essential invariants: Unread is a server-side relationship projection for the current user, not local client state. content_revision advances only for user-visible Issue content, status, Workflow, Runtime, or Delivery changes. Reordering, listing, and marking read do not advance it. read_revisions reuses the LoopItem metadata_json, keyed by user ID with the last read content_revision; no database table is added. The formula is fixed: an absent read cursor or read_revision < content_revision means unread. A meaningful update aligns the actor's read cursor in the same transaction, so a user's own edit does not immediately become unread. Mark-read must ensure a missing or invalid read_revisions value is an object and update one user's JSON path in the same database expression. It must not read and overwrite the entire metadata_json, discard other users' cursors, increment the LoopItem optimistic-lock version, or change business updated_at. The Issue changed event only invalidates projections and is never unread truth. List and detail APIs restore correct state after reconnects or cross-device access.

Scope: when Wework opens a cloud project-space board, one authoritative snapshot request loads the Issues, task bindings, members, and visible agents required by first-screen rendering and interaction. Edge Code owner Board → snapshot API wework/src/features/todo/CloudTodoWorkspace.tsx, wework/src/api/deliveries.ts Snapshot API → aggregate read backend/app/api/endpoints/cloud_projects.py, backend/app/services/project_board_snapshot.py Issues → batch task bindings backend/app/services/loop_items/service.py Snapshot → frontend state wework/src/features/todo/CloudTodoWorkspace.tsx Invariants: opening one cloud board issues exactly one HTTP request for first-screen business data; the snapshot contains every Issue visible to the current user, all active task bindings for those Issues, project members, and active agents visible to the current user; task bindings are read in one project-level batch and never through per-card N+1 requests; the frontend commits first-screen dependency state only after the complete snapshot succeeds, and a cancelled or stale project request never overwrites the active project; Issue events and the 15-second fallback poll reload this same snapshot contract and never restore split requests; non-first-screen detail data such as attachments, comments, and deliveries remains lazy-loaded.

Wegent acts as a constrained OAuth 2 authorization server that proves the current user's identity to registered external clients. External access tokens may read only the dedicated userinfo resource and grant no Wegent API or downstream business permissions. See the External OAuth 2.0 Integration Guide for client registration, PKCE, token exchange, refresh, and revocation.

Responsibility Owner OAuth protocol endpoints and errors backend/app/api/endpoints/oauth_provider.py Clients, codes, JWTs, and refresh rotation backend/app/services/auth/oauth_provider.py OAuth request, response, and Kind schemas backend/app/schemas/oauth_provider.py Refresh-token persistence backend/app/models/oauth_refresh_token.py Developer self-service Client API backend/app/api/endpoints/oauth_clients.py Administrator Client governance API backend/app/api/endpoints/admin/oauth_clients.py Automatic provider-level SigningKey / TokenIssuer provisioning backend/app/services/auth/outbound_token_service.py Client management and consent UI frontend/src/features/settings/, frontend/src/app/auth/oauth/authorize/

External access tokens may access OAuth userinfo only; existing Wegent JWT, API-key, and task-token authentication must reject them. Userinfo returns only id, user_name, and email; it never returns roles, auth sources, preferences, Git data, or resource permissions. Audience is fixed to wegent-userinfo, scope is fixed to userinfo.read, and clients cannot expand either. Authorization server metadata is published at the RFC 8414 location derived from the issuer, and exposes an OAuth-specific JWKS. External OAuth Provider APIs consistently use the /external/oauth prefix and do not share a namespace with Wegent login authentication or internal TokenIssuer APIs. SigningKey and TokenIssuer are OAuth Provider-level configuration, not OAuth Client configuration. The backend must reuse the same eligible signing resources and atomically create them when first needed; the TokenIssuer access-token maximum is fixed at 3600 seconds and must not depend on Client input. An OAuth Client belongs to the developer who created it through Kind.user_id. Ordinary users may list, update, rotate, and delete only their own clients, and client names need to be unique only within one owner. Administrators globally list, disable, and delete clients; they do not register applications or hold client secrets on behalf of developers. Provider protocol resolution searches every active OAuth Client by public client_id; it must not be restricted to clients owned by the system user. OAuth Client create and update APIs must not accept TokenIssuer or token TTL configuration; each Client manages only its own client id, secret, redirect URIs, and enabled state. JWT access tokens follow RFC 9068: they use typ=at+jwt and include and validate iss, sub, aud, exp, iat, jti, client_id, and scope. Redirect URIs match registered values exactly; authorization codes require well-formed PKCE S256, expire quickly, and are consumed once. Token and revocation endpoints allow exactly one client authentication method and reject requests combining HTTP Basic with body credentials. A client's access-token TTL cannot exceed its TokenIssuer limit; a referenced TokenIssuer cannot be deleted or changed to another audience. Authorization errors may redirect with the original state only after both the client and redirect URI are trusted; otherwise the provider returns a local error to prevent open redirects. Refresh tokens are stored only as hashes and rotate on every use; replay revokes the entire family. The RFC 7009 revocation endpoint accepts token_type_hint and returns success for unknown tokens without revealing token state. Disabling or deleting a client, rotating its secret, changing its type, or changing its TokenIssuer revokes its existing refresh tokens. Disabled users, clients, TokenIssuers, or SigningKeys cannot issue or refresh tokens. The consent page cannot be framed, does not leak Referer data, and is not cached. Logs never contain access tokens, refresh tokens, authorization codes, client secrets, or Authorization headers.

No new database columns, unique index, manual cleanup SQL, or bulk migration are required. Deploy the backend and frontend, then reconnect Wework to establish record-scoped online routes. Complete the backend rollout before verifying: connections maintained by old servers do not exercise the new routing. Normal registration and user-requested removal still update records through application APIs.

New Wework installations persist a UUIDv4 device_id. Restarts preserve it. Existing IDs, including local-device, and explicit configurations remain unchanged. runtime_instance_id identifies the persistent Runtime installation; app_device_id identifies its desktop IPC exposure. App records expose execution_target_id as app-record-<primary key> for exact routing. The UI still displays the registered device ID. App WebSocket registration sessions, execution queue pulls, and wake-up rooms must use the same confirmed app-record-<primary key>. Pulling with app_device_id cannot identify a unique record when installations share an IPC alias, and causes Runner is no longer authorized before an Issue starts. Reconnect the Executor after deploying this fix to refresh existing sessions; device removal and historical record changes are unnecessary. The desktop collaboration-app-queue-identity checkpoint starts two real Executors sharing an alias and verifies automatic cloud Issue execution, completion, record routing, and exactly one execution. Configuration creation is file-locked and atomically persisted. Corrupt or unwritable configuration fails explicitly; it never invents a shared fallback identity. Registration matches the owner, default namespace, device ID, Runtime and IPC identities. Identical historical duplicates reuse a stable record; distinct installations retain separate records, online states and execution routes. Ambiguous identities are rejected, never guessed from display names. An existing owner-row transaction lock serializes registration. A Redis lock covers the registration-to-online transition and deletion, without a schema change.

The card menu asks for confirmation and submits the record primary key. Wework, remote and local devices must be offline with no unfinished tasks to be removed. Only cloud devices may be removed while online or busy. Both deletion endpoints recheck ownership and these rules. Protected online or busy records return a conflict; foreign records return not found. Removal only deactivates the selected registration. Task history and local files remain intact. Reconnecting the same installation can restore its record. Historical task, project and default-device references are not bulk rewritten. A unique legacy ID resolves to its record. An ambiguous ID shared by different installations requires an explicit device choice; it must not silently launch on another installation. Removal is not an installation migration.

Plugin installation, updates, acknowledgements and marketplace reads share one device identity: app-record-<primary key> for app devices and logical IDs for other devices. Confirmed aliases of one installation are coalesced using the latest sync result on reads and reconciled on subsequent writes, preserving failures and retry counts without clearing user plugin directories. Successful updates require the device's actual release to match the target; HTTP success or an old installed state alone is insufficient. Desktop uninstall immediately refreshes detail installation state. Both backend and desktop must be released; publishing only a plugin package cannot fix host state management. The desktop plugin-auto-update checkpoint covers upgrades using generated minimal plugin packages, cancellation, catalog refresh, uninstall, reinstall and six-plugin background updates. macOS idle tasks include reclaimable file cache in available memory to avoid indefinitely deferring updates despite sufficient memory. Each generated test package contains a manifest and two skill text files. Real publication and installation verify changed, added and removed skills, plus old version directory cleanup, without historical business packages or binary archives.

Use isolated databases, Redis, users and Electron profiles, never production databases or personal Wework windows. Scenario Expected result Concurrent registration and reconnect Three real Socket.IO registrations create one row; reconnect reuses its key Legacy duplicates Seed identical and distinct Runtime records sharing an ID; match exactly and isolate heartbeat and online states; keep app remote control disabled Remove and restore Reject online Wework and foreign removal; UI confirmation removes only the clicked offline row; reconnect restores its key Device-type removal rules Reject online Wework, remote and local deletion in menus and both APIs; allow confirmed online cloud removal; disable confirmation when a device reconnects UUID persistence UUIDv4 on first start; stable across restarts and concurrent startup; separate homes differ; legacy IDs remain; corrupt configuration fails Historical references Resolve unique old IDs without guessing ambiguous ones or rewriting task JSON Conversation and desktop Device-page chat response and follow-up; real desktop registration exposes a UUID and record route The platform chromium shards run frontend/e2e/tests/devices/app-device-identity.spec.ts. The first shard also runs backend/tests/integration/device_registration_mysql.py against real MySQL. It synchronizes two owners' first identity reads before their inserts and verifies that eight first registrations for one owner still create one row. Registration relies on the existing owner row lock without a redundant Kind range lock, avoiding cross-owner insert deadlocks under REPEATABLE READ. The registration service finishes the authentication read transaction before locking the owner and commits registration independently. Identity reads then use a fresh snapshot, including when all eight callers had already established authentication snapshots. The database-wide isolation level stays unchanged. The executor-chromium job runs the app conversation in tasks/agent-conversation-regression.spec.ts. Desktop CI covers the existing shared-runner remote-device-onboarding checkpoint. Unit tests cover ownership, unfinished-task protection, historical references and concurrent persistence. Report actual execution results separately; adding coverage is not evidence that it passed.

Agents store environment and model requirements. Executors claim eligible work from a durable queue. The first successful claim binds the entire Issue to one environment; comments, replies, retries, and automations retain that binding. Changing a personal default or Agent configuration never moves an existing Issue.

The project settings sidebar groups basic information, execution environments, and automatic processing under Project settings. AI team provides separate Agents, Members, and Collaboration teams pages. Project pages no longer nest participant tabs. Add member and Add agent actions during Issue creation open the corresponding sidebar page directly. Cloud and local projects share this navigation. Wework creation and editing use Basic information and Runtime settings tabs. Basic information opens first with the name, save location, and prompt. New agents default to a fixed environment policy. Among authorized environments supporting the runtime, creation prefers the personal default, then the current desktop Executor. If neither matches and only one eligible environment exists, it selects that environment; multiple candidates require a choice. Device transport aliases match the catalog's device_key; the saved policy uses the environment ID. Models prefer the environment's reported default for the runtime, or the sole selectable model when no default exists. Other cases require a choice. Existing agents retain their saved environment and model policies. A clickable environment and model summary appears in the footer. Switching tabs preserves the draft and advanced configuration. Creation initializes these values once and saves explicit fixed rules. Late catalog responses never overwrite manual choices, and changing environments never replaces a selected model. Incomplete historical configurations and execution-selection dialogs do not apply creation defaults. Runtime settings use one environment selector, grouping devices by personal or workspace ownership and placing automatic project allocation and selection at run time under Other allocation rules. The model selector stays mounted and is disabled until an allocation rule and, for a fixed policy, a specific device are selected. Concrete models and selection at run time share one selector. Options show the model name and cloud/native source. Native selections show the environment account source. Public cloud models do not show a "public account" hint: gateway calls use the signed-in user's identity. Changing environments never replaces a selected model. Invalid environments and models stay visible, and confirmed conflicts also appear on the basic tab and prevent saving. Advanced settings retain both following the execution environment and fixing agent capabilities. Fixed capabilities keep the full plugin, Skill, and MCP configuration, including capabilities referenced by the prompt. Tabs and disclosure change presentation without reducing these rules to one checkbox or changing the saved contract. execution_policy supports project_pool, fixed, and user_select. Backend fixed policies reference a Device Kind ID; local projects use the local environment ID. Ownership is independent of deployment location. model_policy supports fixed and user_select. Models store (runtime, provider, model_id) and source; cloud models additionally store a cloud_model reference containing name, type, namespace, and resource owner ID. Rules never contain model configs or credentials. Historical identities without a source retain native catalog matching and are never silently reinterpreted as cloud models. Environment policy Model catalog Automatic project allocation Authorized cloud models Specific environment Cloud and environment-native models, filtered by runtime support Selection at run time Authorized cloud models Cloud catalogs reuse /api/models/unified and load independently of device catalogs. Execution authorizes the triggering user and resolves cloud accounts through the existing gateway; native models use the environment account. Codex accepts the gateway's three upstream protocols; Claude Code requires Anthropic Messages. Runners report runtimes; native models in historical reports also provide evidence of runtime support. The Executor binds the model gateway to its connected Backend URL, including the scheme, host, port, and path prefix. Stale internal addresses or ports in server configuration are not used as device request addresses. Only the Wegent model gateway path is rebound; direct provider endpoints remain unchanged. Triggering-user credentials and cloud resource identities are preserved. codex_catalog_model_id selects Codex capability metadata independently of the resource identity sent to the gateway. Non-native models receive a capability catalog identity without changing the selected model. Agent details preserve the cloud resource name, type, and owner instead of exposing the upstream model ID as a native model. Manual reruns persist a separate root comment and resolve policies through the comment execution queue, preserving Issue runner affinity. Authorization or configuration failures remain visible. Explicit Team runs resolve the current model selection before building the Bot execution request, without requiring a routed Bot to store another model reference. Comment executions retain the project, Issue, and execution IDs and the board reference before appending the current comment. Agents can read the original Issue through the real board tools. At execution time, preferences.default_execution_target applies only to unbound Issues manually invoking a user_select Agent without an explicit environment. Automations must persist all deferred choices in runnerSelection before being enabled. A collaboration group requires one runner satisfying every member's requirements, while members may use different fixed models. Sharing a personal environment preserves its owner and model account. Project pools intersect workspace and project Device grants. Revoking workspace sharing invalidates project access. Authorization always uses the triggering user; the creator's access is insufficient. Cloud project device pickers distinguish Add from Share and add. Before sharing a personal environment, the UI explains workspace access and account/quota ownership. Clicking the action shares with the workspace before authorizing the project. Submission waits for known sharing status; already shared devices go directly to project authorization. Sharing failures stop the flow. If project authorization fails after sharing succeeds, the UI retains the actual sharing state and retries only project authorization. GET /api/v1/resources/execution-environments?project_id=... exposes the non-secret native catalog reported through runtime.runner.catalog. The last report remains available for offline queueing, with refresh errors visible. Cloud models require runtime support without per-device provider credentials. Manual execution may use the default of an explicitly fixed environment; automatic allocation and environment selection at run time require a cloud model choice. Automations must persist all deferred selections. Local queue claims also recheck cloud access and compile runtime gateway configuration. Device reports and page refreshes use the same catalog contract. Page requests first check environment visibility, then Backend dispatches RPC using the device owner's identity. App environments allow this read-only catalog request through a capability scoped to runtime.runner.catalog; other remote-control permissions follow their existing rules. Refresh failures retain the RPC error code, and invalid catalog responses report runner_catalog_invalid. Logs contain environment IDs, error codes, and exception types without model credentials or RPC contents. Local projects use their local Executor's catalog and durable queue. Backend projects may authorize personal computers and existing servers. Sharing a runner does not share a conversation: each root comment has an independent Runtime task, while thread replies enqueue a new turn on that thread's task. Collaboration dispatch IDs and manager conversation IDs have separate roles. Queue claims, heartbeats, and dispatch outcomes retain codex-queue-{execution_id}. Issue task bindings and initial planning activities point to the actual codex-queue-{execution_id}-manager-initial conversation. Completion, failure, and requeue projections use the same conversation association. Existing detail links containing a dispatch ID resolve through authorized project, Issue, device, and execution records without rewriting historical database rows. Reads still use the execution owner's identity; client-supplied runtime handles never expand access. Invalid Runtime transcript payloads return an explicit 502 error and log field locations without conversation content. Manager plan and status-decision activities store their actual conversation and device and create an Issue session binding. Replies validate the current group assignment and resolve the conversation belonging to that activity. Historical activities without a session identity are resolved from the persisted rounds of the same dispatch. An explicitly recorded older conversation never moves to the latest session; invalid associations return a conflict. Replies to a continuation answer retain that answer's recorded model selection and conversation. Manager replies enter the durable queue with the Issue's bound environment, original conversation, and group dispatch authority. The reply author's permissions and every member's environment and model requirements are checked again. Claiming recompiles member profiles and passes them through the existing continuation API. Materialized member credentials remain in process memory: index refresh preserves the current process's profiles without writing them to the session index. A missing conversation returns an explicit error; saving a comment alone does not count as a successful AI execution. Member tasks are created inside Executor without a separate ordinary execution record for each task. Member activities store their real device and conversation and create an Issue session binding in the same transaction. Replies resolve the conversation through the root dispatch, round, assignment, and member identity and verify that device aliases refer to the same environment. They enter the durable queue and continue that member's conversation with its model requirements, without switching to the manager. Missing assignments or mismatched session identities return an explicit conflict. Details for historical member cards without a session binding authorize access through persisted assignments. This does not modify historical data or require the current model catalog. Reading a historical conversation does not require the group to remain the current assignment; executing a reply does. Client-supplied runtime handles cannot expand read authority.

Environment authorization is independent of directory preparation. Creating Issues, assigning Agents, and entering the queue require no manual initialization. Local projects no longer use preparation records as authorization. The environment page shows device availability without a global initialized badge. More → Prepare project directory ahead of time remains optional. Runner routing selects an execution device without creating a code-project binding. Projects without repositories or setup commands use an independent session directory; configured project preparation supplies the directory when needed. Git worktrees require a repository or a valid code workspace. Local assignment also requires no preinitialized directory; existing preparation records are only reusable state. Fixed native models do not request the cloud catalog, so cloud outages cannot block their assignment. After claiming work, Runtime saves a snapshot of repositories, setup commands, and the configuration fingerprint. It prepares the directory asynchronously before creating an isolated worktree or using the shared directory. Automatic and optional preparation share the Executor implementation and serialize access to each directory. Successful fingerprints are reused; changed configurations give new tasks a new directory. Historical paths are reused only on their original runner. Cloning uses Git credentials configured on the environment, including access to private repositories. While preparation is pending, task creation returns workspacePending: true and an empty workspacePath. Runtime persists the final directory and updates the local execution binding. Preparation consumes a running slot and supports cancellation without blocking task acceptance or heartbeats. Repository and setup failures retain actionable errors without starting a model session. After repairing the environment, retrying the same task uses its saved snapshot; after editing project configuration, a new execution uses the new configuration. Restored queued work and force-started work also pass through preparation. Replies retain their session directory. Existing sessions and workflows inheriting an upstream workspace do not prepare a new directory when configuration changes. Issue runner bindings remain stable, and cancelling preparation never deletes a shared project directory.

Device lists keep in-memory snapshots scoped to the API session and project or workspace. Reopening displays the last successful result immediately and refreshes in the background. Only a list without a snapshot shows a local skeleton. Failed refreshes retain devices and show an inline error with retry; a successful empty response clears the snapshot. Successful edits update it immediately, and older reads cannot overwrite those edits. Subscribers share in-flight requests. Project devices and workspace devices load independently. Sharing provenance is not inferred until the workspace catalog arrives. Personal candidate resources load when Add device opens; the Git repository catalog loads when Project setup expands. An unloaded candidate catalog does not mean no devices are online. Snapshots serve display only; existing server and Executor checks still authorize execution. Loading unit tests cover reopening, slow requests, initial failure, failed refresh and retry, empty results, API-session and project isolation, request deduplication, and edits racing with older reads. The existing desktop CI environment fixture also checks navigating away and immediately returning. The collaboration device page and device picker share session snapshots of the device catalog without loading the full resource catalog containing agents. Cloud discovery reuses the Cloud work GET /api/devices endpoint and executor filtering; local discovery reads local devices directly. The sources load independently, so slow navigation or cloud requests do not block local devices. Stable device identities deduplicate records, with registered cloud records supplying device IDs for authorization. Cloud projects and workspaces use registered cloud device IDs; local projects and workspaces use the local catalog. Local placeholder IDs cannot become cloud grants. Personal and workspace candidates render independently, with errors and retry for failed sources instead of false empty results. Catalogs are isolated by API session and shared across project API wrappers in the same session; switching accounts does not reuse the previous catalog. Existing desktop CI scenarios cover cached devices when reopening the device page and picker. The current device is identified by the stable device identity reported by the local runtime, never by the local/app deployment type or display name. Other computers and historical records use cloud device management. Device catalogs and environment lists place a known current device first, followed by online, provisioning, error, and offline states, with natural name sorting and ID tie-breaking. Historical records with the same name but different identities remain distinct.

Workspace Maintainers/Owners can register an existing server in the environment UI or call: POST /api/v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}/runners {"name": "Team execution server"} The response contains environment_id, device_id, and a token displayed once. Configure the existing wegent-executor service with: EXECUTOR_MODE=local WEGENT_BACKEND_URL=<Backend URL> DEVICE_ID=<registered device_id> WEGENT_AUTH_TOKEN=<returned token> local is the existing Executor transport mode. The environment's deploymentLocation=cloud denotes server deployment; workspaceOwnerId denotes ownership independently. The runner uses an independent machine identity, not the administrator's login. The token authorizes only its registered device; only its digest is stored. Project actions inside a task use the triggering user's authorization. Model credentials remain on the server. Codex reports its native model catalog. Claude reports explicitly configured models from WEGENT_CLAUDE_HOME/settings.json (default ~/.claude/settings.json). Custom Claude services automatically derive a provider identity from the SHA-256 digest of the normalized endpoint, without additional configuration. Existing env.WEGENT_CLAUDE_PROVIDER_ID values remain explicit identities. Normalization removes URL usernames, passwords, and fragments while keeping protocol, port, path, and query differences distinct. Changing URL userinfo does not change the provider identity; endpoint addresses and credentials are not included in catalog reports. Account configuration still belongs to the execution environment. Revoke with DELETE /api/v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}/runners/{environment_id}. This disables the environment and disconnects its socket. Subsequent events and connections reject the old token. Registering again creates a new environment without migrating bound Issues.

Condition Behavior Offline or busy Remain queued with a reason; resume when available; allow cancellation Project or sharing permission revoked Block claiming with an authorization error Model removed or provider changed Require model/environment configuration repair Bound Issue conflicts with a new fixed policy ISSUE_RUNNER_CONFLICT; never switch runners Missing manual choice Return a structured selection request and replay after selection Missing automation choice Reject enabling; never read personal defaults Invalid local queued configuration Show waiting_runtime; repair, cancel the old execution, and resubmit Backend binds and claims within one transaction using an Issue row lock and conditional update. Local queues use SQLite IMMEDIATE transactions. Execution records retain the final runner, native model, account label, and configuration sources without credentials. Starting a direct local execution atomically marks its comment as running and its Issue as in progress, including continued threads. Queued replies keep the Issue in progress until the last turn finishes and moves it to review. Group manager and member executions leave Issue state to their workflow.

This feature reuses existing extension fields. It adds no tables or columns and performs no bulk data migration: Data Storage Agent environment and model policies Project Agent metadata, or Bot CRD spec Personal default environment User preferences.default_execution_target Environment model and account-source catalog Device CRD spec.runnerCatalog Issue environment binding Issue metadata.runner_binding.environment_id Execution policy snapshot and version Routing object in the existing execution_payload: Backend runtime_selection.runner_routing, local runnerRouting Actual environment, model, and configuration sources Selection and routing snapshots in the same payload, plus existing Runtime identity fields First claim uses an Issue row lock and conditional JSON path update in the execution claim transaction, preserving other metadata. ORM content updates protect committed affinity against stale metadata writes. Local claiming uses the existing SQLite IMMEDIATE transaction and JSON path update; the local schema version remains 10. Queue queries identify routing objects within the existing payload after applying status and device filters, without a dedicated routing column. Existing explicit Agent device, model, and runtime configuration remains in its original fields. For historical Issues without a JSON binding, read prior executions and TaskBindings. Backend resolves device aliases within their owner; local storage uses durable device IDs. An unambiguous historical binding is saved on the first valid claim. Unresolved devices or conflicting history require correction rather than adopting a personal default. Existing JSON bindings remain authoritative. Focused coverage includes policy combinations, model catalogs, revoked access, concurrent first claims, JSON preservation and rollback, historical affinity, original-schema queries, separate root sessions, queued replies, and machine credentials. Existing CI scenarios using native model fixtures choose a fixed environment and assert that automatic allocation does not expose those models. Cloud and native model routing also need separate gateway and account validation. Do not run E2E or AI verify without an explicit user request. Preparation tests cover first use, concurrent reuse, configuration changes, failure and retry, cancellation during setup, cloning before isolated worktrees, restored queues, and forced starts. Existing CI scenarios no longer initialize environments as a prerequisite; the remote scenario retains optional preparation failure and recovery coverage. Run E2E and isolated packaged-app AI verification when explicitly requested and retain actual results. Only model services are mocked; backend, queue, and Executor implementations remain real. Provisioning cloud machines, moving Issues between runners, and cost-based scheduling remain outside scope. Python/Rust API ownership and Rust cutover rules are unchanged.

A persisted history file can outgrow the 980,000-byte cloud Runtime response limit, even after gzip and base64 encoding. Protocol 2 adds lossless chunks to the existing runtime.tasks.transcript RPC so a transport failure does not appear as an empty chat.

New clients explicitly request transcriptProtocolVersion: 2. New Executors retain the original response for absent versions and version 1. Unknown versions fail explicitly. A new client accepts a legacy response when an old Executor ignores the additional field. The old Executor's payload limit still applies. Direct RPC reads need support in both client and Executor. For HTTP reads, Backend requests device protocol 2: explicit v2 clients receive chunks, while absent versions and version 1 receive the original JSON reconstructed by Backend. The device must support v2 to read histories above its limit. The main conversation and Issue panes share the transcript client, loading the latest 5 turns and using cursors for older pages. For protocol 2, the Executor defaults an unspecified page size to 5. Explicit limit values retain the existing pagination behavior, including navigation and test overrides. Existing Codex turn/item cursors, provider compatibility and live merging retain their semantics. Protocol 2 projects full tool content for the page it reads; fullContent: false still means that only a page was loaded. Exports use includeFullContent: true and no longer silently stop at 500 turns.

Issue conversations carrying projectSession read through the existing HTTP endpoint. For every chunk, the backend checks project access and the Issue's persistent session binding, then forwards the RPC using the bound device, task and session address. It preserves transcriptProtocolVersion, transcriptTransfer, pagination and refresh fields. The response model retains chunk fields for the shared client's validation and decompression. Revoking access during a transfer fails the request without publishing a partial page. For HTTP callers that do not request v2, Backend collects device chunks within one HTTP request, verifies the snapshot SHA-256, offsets and complete size, then decompresses and restores string references. The response retains canonical turns, messages and page cursors. Explicit pagination, refresh and export fields are retained; an omitted page size uses the v2 default of 5 turns. Every internal continuation reauthorizes the original caller. Each packet checks permission, Issue visibility, binding and device ownership in its own short Session, closed before waiting for the device RPC. This avoids reusing a MySQL REPEATABLE READ snapshot or ORM state without committing or rolling back the caller's Session. A separately committed revocation or visibility restriction returns 404 before the next RPC, and no collected partial history is returned. Compressed snapshots, decompressed JSON and projected restored JSON are each limited to 64 MiB. Before restoration, Backend counts compact UTF-8 JSON bytes for every expanded string reference, including repeated references and escaping, and rejects oversized pages before restoration or model validation. The entire aggregation shares the existing transcript RPC timeout budget. Invalid packets or an overall timeout return 502. Logs include device error codes, chunk offsets and byte counts with the existing request ID, without history contents. The device's 980,000-byte limit remains unchanged. Failed pagination preserves visible messages and the current cursor, so retry reads the same page. Closing or switching the pane prevents stale requests from updating another conversation. Every chunk carries the original projectSession through HTTP project authorization. Each response contains success: true, transcriptProtocolVersion: 2, and transfer: Field Meaning snapshotId SHA-256 identity of the complete gzip snapshot encoding gzip+base64+json offset This chunk's byte offset in the gzip stream nextOffset Next offset, or null for the final chunk totalBytes Complete gzip snapshot size payload Base64-encoded bytes for this chunk Continuations add transcriptTransfer: { snapshotId, offset } to the original request. Each chunk contains at most 360 KiB of bytes. Base64 and metadata remain below 512 KiB, avoiding outer compression and the 980,000-byte cloud limit. Chunk boundaries can cross UTF-8 characters; clients decompress and parse only after receiving the complete stream. The gzip payload is { transcript, strings, references }. Strings of at least 1,024 bytes are interned in a shared table. Explicit paths and table indexes restore their null placeholders. This removes repeated transmission of tool content in messages, runtime items and turns without removing logical fields. Clients validate consistent snapshot identity, contiguous offsets and final size; gzip verifies content integrity. Incomplete pages never reach conversation state.

Multipart snapshots are stored alongside the Runtime index at runtime-work/transcript-transfers/<SHA-256 of task/session address>/<snapshotId>.gz. They are scoped to the task and requested session. Without an explicit session, publication resolves the task's linked session after reading. Writes are atomic, and continuations need no process-local state. Reads can continue after Executor restart if the address is unchanged and the snapshot has not expired. Single-chunk responses do not write files. Snapshots expire after 24 hours and are removed on subsequent protocol 2 history reads. Expired or cross-session reads, invalid offsets, disk errors and corrupt data fail explicitly and require reloading history. The main pane shows the error and a reload action while preserving visible messages. RPC completion logging now happens after outer encoding, so payload-limit failures are no longer logged as successful responses. Chunking bounds individual transport packets, not total memory or latency. The rollout reader parses lines on a blocking worker, but still scans the file and retains parsed turns before selecting a page. Very large turns and full exports can still consume substantial memory. The cache has time-based cleanup but no additional disk quota. Original history files are never rewritten by this protocol.

Conversation search applies the rendered prose and process-block visibility rules and locates matches by their original item IDs. Loading a match retains its complete anchor turn, including completed turns: distant final-answer fragments can determine whether a same-text process block is hidden. Neighboring turns remain paginated. Temporary context pages do not add matches to completed provider search results; leaving search restores the original messages and pagination. Anchor size still depends on the turn. Cloud search runs in the Rust Backend and checks project access, Issue visibility, persisted session bindings and device identity before calling the Executor. Bound reads discard client-supplied workspace paths and runtime handles. Duplicate prose, long turns, context continuation and restoration run through the existing local running-conversation-history and cloud conversation-state CI checkpoints. Scenario Expected result Mixed client/Executor versions Legacy HTTP JSON remains readable over device chunks; unknown versions fail High-entropy output, Unicode and structured results Exact reconstruction over multiple bounded packets Missing/reordered chunks, changed snapshot, corrupt gzip or expiry Explicit failure without publishing a partial page Continuation under another task/session Snapshot cannot be read from another address More than 500 turns Complete export and contiguous latest/older pages Failed history load Visible error and reload action Tests cover Rust transport and Codex pagination, the shared TypeScript decoder, desktop IPC and conversation UI. The existing registered running-conversation-history desktop checkpoint includes high-entropy tool output and checks restart hydration, complete tool history and multipart snapshot content through its existing CI entry point. HTTP and project authorization tests cover chunk fields, invalid requests and access revocation during a transfer. The collaboration-issue-task-discovery checkpoint reads oversized tool output through the project HTTP path without loss and reopens the Issue pane after reload. The same checkpoint verifies full oversized output through an HTTP request without a protocol version. Backend tests cover version 1, mid-transfer revocation, corrupt snapshots, resource bounds and the overall timeout. Run E2E and ai:verify only when explicitly requested.

A local run exercised the production code with a 77,796,060-byte rollout containing 4,326 records. Parsing recovered 19 turns and 1,173 completed items. The four history pages matched the full turn sequence without omissions or duplicates. The shared TypeScript client decoded actual Rust response packets; all six cases matched the original logical responses field for field. Request Original single gzip/base64 response New chunks Largest chunk response Latest 5 turns 270,575 bytes 1 116,038 bytes Previous 5 turns 3,149,525 bytes 3 491,758 bytes All 19 turns 4,262,662 bytes 4 491,760 bytes Sizes include protocol response fields. The original responses above the 980,000-byte limit demonstrate that reducing turn count alone does not prevent oversized responses. The offline run covered local parsing, response projection, disk snapshot continuation and cross-language decoding. A subsequent isolated Electron run imported the same file and loaded 5 → 10 → 15 → 19 turns, showing 38 user/assistant messages without a history error. All pages loaded again after a renderer reload, and the latest five turns recovered after a Runtime restart. A live cloud connection and the full E2E suite were not tested. Private history and temporary test entry points are excluded from the repository.

From the repository root, use the existing isolated verification launcher: pnpm --filter wework ai:verify start --rollout /absolute/path/to/rollout.jsonl --timeout 180000 The launcher builds the current app and Executor, copies the history into an isolated test directory, and seeds a Rollout replay project and task binding. Only the copied initial workspace metadata changes; subsequent history records and the source file remain byte-identical. No conversation is sent and no historical command is replayed. This option cannot be combined with --codex-home-initialization true or --executor-home. Open the conversation under Rollout replay and verify: The latest history appears without an empty-chat placeholder or loading error. Older pages load, including the large tool output on the preceding page. This case contains 19 turns in total. Switching away or reloading the window preserves recoverable history. History remains readable after restarting the isolated Runtime. Use the session path printed by the launcher in these commands: pnpm --filter wework ai:verify reload --session /path/from/start/session.json pnpm --filter wework ai:verify restart-core-dsh --session /path/from/start/session.json pnpm --filter wework ai:verify stop --session /path/from/start/session.json The final command ends the test session. Logs are next to session.json; multipart snapshots are under executor-home/runtime-work/transcript-transfers/. This checks the desktop UI and real local IPC. Verify cloud Socket.IO separately on a test cloud device.
